spots.name: Dōtonbori
spots.label: Dotonbori

text.geographic_location: Dōtonbori is in the Namba district of Osaka's Chūō ward, along the Dōtonbori canal between Dōtonboribashi Bridge and Nipponbashi Bridge.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Namba district in Chūō ward and follow the Dōtonbori canal. From there the subject is 14 m to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 15 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: Dōtonbori is an open public district with streets and a canal-side walkway; individual shops, restaurants and attractions have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Dōtonbori is Osaka's famous food-and-entertainment strip, where giant lit-up signs crowd the streets and reflect in the canal. That mix of colour, movement and water is what makes it work so well on a phone. The canal was begun in 1612 and finished in 1615. In 1621 the area was set aside as Osaka's entertainment district, and by 1662 it had six Kabuki and five Bunraku theatres. Today the theatres have mostly gone, but the showbusiness feel lives on in the signs. Look for the Glico runner billboard, often seen as a symbol of Osaka, and the moving crab above the Kani Dōraku restaurants, a sign installed in 1996. The stretch of canal-side walkway between Tazaemonbashi and Ebisubashi opened to the public in 2004, so you can now photograph the buildings from the water's edge as well as from the street. Try one wide shot to show the whole scene, then step in for details such as a single sign, a lantern or a reflection. Expect crowds, so hold the phone steady and keep an eye on people around you. Shoot a few frames in a row, because someone will always walk through the first one.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 15 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. A few steps either side lets you change the angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street scene. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit in tall signs and the canal together, and to telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single signs and details.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the signs are lit and glow in the canal. In the evening it is busiest, so for a clearer view try earlier in the evening.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour instead of washing out to white. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone still against your body or a rail for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the canal edge or the building fronts with them so the picture looks straight. Include some water in the lower part of the frame to catch the reflections, and keep one bold sign as your main subject. If the moving crab sign is in view, try a Live Photo to catch its motion.

spots.alt: Dōtonbori, Osaka: Osaka's famous food-and-entertainment strip. Photo spot

spots.name: Osaka Castle
spots.label: Osaka Castle

text.geographic_location: Osaka Castle is in Chūō-ku, Osaka, and occupies a large walled and moated site of its own.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the castle grounds in Chūō-ku, Osaka. The phone icon on the map is about 620 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The grounds are a large public site, but entry to individual buildings and the keep may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.description: Osaka Castle sits in Chūō-ku and is one of Japan's best-known landmarks. It played a major part in the unification of Japan in the sixteenth century. Toyotomi Hideyoshi began building it in 1583 on the site of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji temple. The main keep is five storeys tall on the outside and eight on the inside, and it stands on a tall stone foundation. For a phone photo, that mix of a high stone base, the tiered keep and the open space around it gives you a clear, layered shape to frame. The stone walls built in the 1620s still stand. They are made of interlocking granite blocks laid without mortar, and many carry the crests of the families who supplied them. These make a good foreground for a photo of the keep. The grounds cover roughly 61,000 square metres and are ringed by moats, so there is plenty of room to move and try different angles. Step back a little if you can, keep your phone upright and watch that the top of the keep is not cut off. Walls, gates and turrets around the grounds also make good close-ups if the keep itself is crowded.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 620 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. The keep rises ahead of you above its stone base.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole keep in from this close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the top storeys or the stone walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or afternoon on a clear day. Facing north from here, the sun is usually behind you and lights the front of the keep. Early on a weekday is likely to be quieter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the keep to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the white walls keep their detail. Take a few frames, since people may walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and hold the phone upright. Use the 0.5x lens so the base and the top of the keep both fit, and keep the vertical lines straight. Include a stretch of the granite wall at the bottom of the frame for depth. Then try 1x or a little zoom for a tighter shot.

spots.alt: Osaka Castle, Osaka: one of Japan's best-known landmarks. Photo spot

spots.name: Umeda Sky Building
spots.label: Umeda Sky Building

text.geographic_location: In Kita-ku, Osaka, on the edge of the Umeda business district, within the Shin-Umeda City area, which also includes The Westin Osaka. It is close to Osaka Station and Umeda Station.
text.directions_text: Start from the Osaka Station and Umeda Station area, which is close to the building on the edge of the Umeda district. Check a map app or ask your hotel for the best way to walk from there. Once you are in Shin-Umeda City, look for the two tall towers joined at the top and head for their base. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.access_note: The base and gardens are part of a mixed-use complex and the rooftop observatory is a separate attraction, so check the official site before you go for access and ticket details.
text.description: The Umeda Sky Building is two 40-storey towers joined near the top by glass bridges, with escalators and lifts crossing an open gap between them. The towers reach 170 m, or 190 m including the spires, and were designed by Hiroshi Hara. The building opened to the public on 25 March 1993. Hara wanted a "floating city", and from the base you can see why. The linked top floors look as if they hang in the air above the gap, which makes a strong, simple shape for a phone photo. At the foot of the towers are the Island Garden and the Vegetable Garden, with walking trails and water features. These give you room to step back and change your angle. The rooftop Floating Garden Observatory is the main attraction inside. Access and ticket rules can change, so check the official site before you go. For photos, tilt the phone upwards and use the gridlines to keep the two towers upright and balanced. Include some of the bridge at the top, as it is the most distinctive part. Wipe your lens first, as finger marks show up badly against bright sky. Step back a little between shots, because a few paces changes how the gap and bridge line up.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look straight up between the towers, then walk a few paces back towards the garden areas at the base for a wider view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so both towers and the top bridge fit in from close to the base. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the glass bridge and escalators at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good time, when the sky is softer and the glass can pick up warm light. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not turn white and the glass keeps its detail. Hold the phone as level as you can before tilting up, and use the gridlines to check the verticals.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the two towers up with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep the glass bridge near the top third of the frame and let the open gap between the towers form the centre of the picture. For a different angle, try a low, upward-tilted shot at the ultra-wide, then a tighter one at the telephoto.

spots.alt: Umeda Sky Building, Osaka: two 40-storey towers joined near the top by glass bridges. Photo spot
